 Explain challenges in maintaining Legacy software.


 Legacy software is older software that was developed decades ago, has been continually modified to meet changes in
 business requirements and computing platforms, and is still business-critical — the organisation cannot simply throw it
 away (Pressman).


Legacy systems are often characterised by poor quality: inextensible designs, convoluted code, poor or non-existent
documentation, and test cases/results that were never archived. Maintaining them is therefore difficult for the following
reasons:

 1. Poor or missing documentation – original design documents are lost or outdated; maintainers must reverse-engineer the
 logic from code.

 2. Obsolete technology – written in old languages (COBOL, FORTRAN, old C) and run on old hardware/OS; skilled
 programmers are rare and expensive.

 3. Convoluted, 'spaghetti' code – years of patches have destroyed the original structure (high coupling, low cohesion), so
 every change risks a side-effect (the ripple effect).
 4. Original developers have left – domain and design knowledge has walked out of the door; nobody fully understands the
 system.

 5. Integration problems – it must interoperate with modern databases, web/mobile front-ends and cloud services for which
 it was never designed.

 6. High cost and risk of change – the system is business-critical, so downtime or a regression is unacceptable; testing is hard
 because test suites were never archived.

 7. Software deterioration – each change introduces new defects before earlier ones are removed, so the failure-rate curve
 keeps rising (software does not wear out, it deteriorates).

 Explain how software engineering practices contribute to improving system reliability. What are some key practices
 that directly influence the reliability of a software system?


 Software reliability is the probability of failure-free operation of a computer program in a specified environment for a
 specified time. It is commonly measured by MTBF = MTTF + MTTR (mean time between failures = mean time to failure +
 mean time to repair).


Software engineering is a layered technology resting on a quality focus: the process, methods and tools layers all exist to
build high-quality — and therefore reliable — software. Reliability is not tested in at the end; it is engineered in throughout
the life cycle.

Key practices that directly influence reliability:

 1. Rigorous requirements engineering – complete, unambiguous, validated requirements remove the largest source of
 defects (wrong or missing behaviour).

 2. Sound design principles – modularity, high cohesion, low coupling, information hiding and defensive design isolate faults
 and prevent ripple effects.

 3. Technical reviews / inspections – walkthroughs and formal technical reviews remove 60–75% of design errors before
 coding (cheaper than testing).

 4. Systematic testing – unit, integration, system and regression testing with boundary-value and path coverage; plus stress
 testing for robustness.
 5. Coding standards and static analysis – avoid error-prone constructs; exception handling and input validation.

 6. Configuration/change management – controlled changes and version control prevent regression and inconsistent builds.

 7. Software quality assurance and metrics – defect tracking, defect-removal efficiency, reliability growth models guide
 improvement.

 8. Fault tolerance – redundancy, check-pointing, graceful degradation for critical systems.


 Example: an ATM switch adopts code inspections, 90% unit-test coverage and regression testing on every release; its
 MTBF rises from 200 h to 2,000 h.

 Q1 (b) 5 Marks CO-2 · SO-1 · BL-L Answer length: ~1–1.5 pages

 To what extent does Scrum contribute to improving team productivity and project success in software engineering?
 Provide evidence or examples to support your evaluation.


Scrum is an agile framework of short time-boxed sprints (2–4 weeks) with three roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master,
Development Team), artifacts (product backlog, sprint backlog, increment) and events (sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint
review, retrospective).

How Scrum improves productivity and success:

 1. Focus and prioritisation – the PO orders the backlog by value, so the team always works on the most valuable items; no
 mid-sprint changes avoids context switching.

 2. Daily Scrum (3 questions) surfaces obstacles within 24 h; the Scrum Master removes impediments → less idle time.
 3. Self-organising, cross-functional team → ownership, motivation, faster decisions.

 4. Frequent delivery and sprint reviews → early customer feedback, less rework, higher customer satisfaction.

 5. Retrospectives → continuous process improvement; velocity typically rises over sprints.

 6. Transparency (burn-down charts, task boards) → realistic forecasting and early risk detection.

Evidence: the Standish Group CHAOS reports consistently show agile projects succeed roughly 3× more often than waterfall
projects (≈ 39–42% vs ≈ 11–14% successful); Jeff Sutherland reports hyper-productive Scrum teams; companies such as
Spotify and many Indian IT firms (Infosys, TCS) adopted Scrum to shorten release cycles.

Extent / limits: gains depend on an empowered PO, a skilled stable team and organisational support; Scrum alone does not
ensure engineering quality (needs CI, testing) and scales poorly without frameworks (Scrum-of-Scrums, SAFe). Hence Scrum
significantly improves productivity and success when practised genuinely, but is not a silver bullet.

 Scoring tip: 'To what extent' → mechanisms + evidence + limits. Keep it to about one page.

Phases of the Waterfall model

 1. Communication – project initiation and requirements gathering: meetings with the customer and stakeholders to
 understand objectives; output is the Software Requirements Specification (SRS), reviewed and signed off.

 2. Planning – estimating effort and cost, scheduling tasks, identifying risks and resources, and defining how progress will be
 tracked; output is the project plan.

 3. Modeling – analysis (data, functional and behavioural models of the requirements) and design (architecture, data
 structures, interfaces and component-level/algorithmic detail); output is the design document.

 4. Construction – code generation (translating design into source code) and testing (unit, integration and system testing) to
 uncover errors.

 5. Deployment – delivery of the product to the customer, support (maintenance: corrective, adaptive, perfective) and
 collection of feedback.

Variant: the V-model depicts the relationship of quality-assurance actions to these phases — as the team moves down the left
side, requirements are refined into detail; moving up the right side, each level of testing validates the corresponding model
(unit test ↔ component design, integration test ↔ architecture, system test ↔ requirements, acceptance test ↔ customer
needs).

Why the Waterfall model is a prescriptive process model

A prescriptive process model 'prescribes' a set of process elements — framework activities, software engineering actions,
tasks, work products, quality-assurance and change-control mechanisms — and a workflow (the order in which these
elements are inter-related). Its goal is to bring order and structure to software development. Waterfall is the purest example
because:

 1. Fixed, predefined sequence: it prescribes a strict linear flow – communication → planning → modeling → construction →
 deployment; a phase starts only after the previous one is complete and signed off.

 2. Defined work products at each phase: SRS, project plan, design document, code, test reports – each acts as a formal
 'gate' (milestone).

 3. Heavy documentation and formality: process is document-driven; documentation is the main means of communication
 and control.

 4. Plan-driven: scope, schedule and cost are fixed early; deviations are handled through formal change control.

Major features of Scrum

 1. Small, self-organising, cross-functional teams that maximise communication and minimise overhead.

 2. Three roles – Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team.

 3. Artifacts: Product Backlog (prioritised list of requirements/features), Sprint Backlog (items selected for the current sprint
 plus tasks), Increment (potentially shippable product) and burn-down charts.

 4. Time-boxed events: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum (15-min meeting; each member answers: what did you do since the last
 meeting? what obstacles are you encountering? what will you accomplish by the next meeting?), Sprint Review (demo to
 stakeholders) and Sprint Retrospective (process improvement).

 5. Sprints of fixed length (typically 30 days in the original method, now 2–4 weeks); no changes are introduced during a
 sprint, giving the team a stable short-term environment.

 6. Demos deliver the software increment to the customer so that functionality can be demonstrated and evaluated.

 7. Empirical process control – transparency, inspection and adaptation; process is adjusted based on what is observed.

 8. Partitioning of work into 'packets' – the process accommodates change, and work is partitioned to deal with uncertainty
 and risk.

Judgement

Adopting CMMI does not necessarily guarantee higher quality. CMMI is an enabler: it raises the probability of consistent

Importance of a comprehensive design before implementation

 1. Cost of change escalates: an error found in design costs ~1 unit to fix, during coding ~6.5 units, during testing ~15 units

Critical note

A comprehensive design is only as good as the requirements; if requirements change, a rigid up-front design becomes a
liability – which is why the waterfall model is advised only when requirements are well understood. Over-designing (analysis
paralysis) can also delay delivery.


 Example: In a payroll system, if the design omits a 'tax-rule' component and hard-codes tax slabs in several modules,

Critical discussion

(i) Balancing conflicting needs. Stakeholders pull in different directions — marketing wants many features, finance wants low
cost, users want simplicity, security wants strict controls. Negotiation (e.g., Boehm's win-win model: identify key stakeholders

(ii) Resolving ambiguity. Natural-language statements such as 'the system should respond quickly' are untestable. RE converts
them to measurable form ('95% of searches return within 2 s'), builds models and prototypes, and uses reviews to catch
vague words ('user-friendly', 'etc.', 'as appropriate').

(iii) Ensuring feasibility. Technical, economic, schedule and operational feasibility are checked during inception/negotiation so
that the team does not commit to something impossible within budget or technology.

Influence on architectural decisions

 1. Separation of OLTP and OLAP: large information systems adopt a layered/data-centred architecture in which operational
 databases serve transactions while a central warehouse serves analytics – so heavy queries do not slow down
 transactions.

 2. Data-centred (repository) style: the warehouse becomes the central repository accessed by many client tools (reporting,
 dashboards, mining engines) – architecture is chosen around the data store.

 3. Data-flow (pipe-and-filter) pipelines: ETL processes are naturally modelled as filters: extract → clean → transform → load
 → mine.

 4. Scalability and performance: volume and history drive choices such as distributed storage, partitioning, data marts per
 department, caching, and batch vs. real-time loading.

 5. Quality attributes: security (sensitive data consolidation), availability, and data quality become explicit architectural
 concerns.

 6. Business intelligence components: mining algorithms (classification, clustering, association rules) become separate
 analytic components consuming the warehouse.

How these concepts guide database design

(a) Architectural level – decisions about the overall data organisation: which databases exist (operational DBs, staging area,
enterprise warehouse, departmental data marts), how they are integrated, how data flows between them, and which
subsystem owns which data. The warehouse design is subject-oriented and integrated rather than application-specific.

(b) Component level – designing the data structures that individual software components use. Pressman's principles for
component-level data design:

 1. Apply systematic analysis principles to data as well as to function and behaviour.

 2. Identify all data structures and the operations to be performed on each.

 3. Establish a data dictionary and use it to define both data and program design.

 4. Defer low-level data design decisions until late in the design process.

 5. Know the representation of a data structure only to modules that use it directly (information hiding).

 6. Develop a library of useful data structures and the operations applicable to them.

 7. The design and programming language should support specification and realisation of abstract data types.


 Example – e-commerce company: the order-processing DB (normalised OLTP) feeds a nightly ETL into a star-schema

 recommendation module uses a hash-map of product-id → related-products, hidden behind an interface.

 Fig P2-7 — Levels of testing: each level verifies a corresponding development artefact (V-model view).


1. Unit testing

Tests each component individually – module interface, local data structures, boundary conditions, independent paths, error-
handling paths – using drivers and stubs. White-box focused; done by developers.

2. Integration testing

Combines unit-tested components according to the design and tests their interfaces: top-down (stubs), bottom-up (drivers,
clusters), sandwich; regression and smoke testing accompany it.

3. Validation testing

Checks that the software functions in a manner reasonably expected by the customer (as per SRS validation criteria). Includes
configuration review, alpha testing (at developer's site by end users) and beta testing (at customer sites, without developer),
and acceptance tests.

4. System testing

Tests the software together with other system elements (hardware, people, databases): recovery testing (forces failure,
checks recovery), security testing (verifies protection mechanisms), stress testing (abnormal quantity/frequency/volume of
resources), performance testing (run-time performance in integrated context) and deployment (configuration) testing.

 define software quality?


The ISO 9126 standard was developed to identify the key quality attributes for computer software. It defines six key quality
characteristics, each refined into sub-characteristics that can be measured through internal and external metrics:

 Characteristic Definition (ISO 9126 / Pressman) Sub-characteristics

 Functionality Degree to which the software satisfies stated needs. Suitability, accuracy, interoperability,
 compliance, security

 Reliability Amount of time the software is available for use. Maturity, fault tolerance, recoverability

 Usability Degree to which the software is easy to use. Understandability, learnability, operability

 Efficiency Degree to which the software makes optimal use of system Time behaviour, resource behaviour
 resources.

 Maintainability Ease with which repair may be made to the software. Analysability, changeability, stability, testability

 Portability Ease with which the software can be transposed from one Adaptability, installability, conformance,
 environment to another. replaceability


How efficiency defines quality

 Time behaviour – response time, throughput, processing time (e.g., search results in < 2 s).

 Resource behaviour – CPU, memory, battery, bandwidth, storage used.

 An efficient product feels fast, scales to more users per server and costs less to operate; inefficiency directly degrades user
 satisfaction (e.g., slow mobile apps are uninstalled).

How maintainability defines quality

 Analysability – ease of diagnosing deficiencies or causes of failure.

 Changeability – effort to implement modifications.

 Stability – low risk of unexpected effects after modification.

 Testability – effort to validate the modified software.

 Since most of a product's life-cycle cost is maintenance, high maintainability means faster bug fixes, cheaper
 enhancements and longer useful life (measured e.g. by MTTChange, cyclomatic complexity, modularity).

How portability defines quality

 Adaptability – can run in different environments without change (Windows/Linux/cloud, browsers, screen sizes).
 Installability – effort to install in a given environment.

 Conformance – adheres to portability standards/conventions.

 Replaceability – can replace another specified product in that environment.

 A portable product reaches more users and survives platform changes (e.g., a web app that works on any browser, a Java
 app on any JVM).

Overall: ISO 9126 defines quality not as a single value but as a profile across characteristics; efficiency reflects operational
quality, maintainability reflects quality over change, and portability reflects quality across environments. (ISO 9126 has since
been superseded by ISO/IEC 25010, which adds security and compatibility as separate characteristics.)
